practice.title: June as a Purification Retreat
agreedSteps: Bring an intention to purify into all of our Dharma activities — viewing everything we do as an opponent force against negative karma.

When daily anxieties arise, remember what we really should be concerned about: the certainty of lower rebirth if negative karma is not purified. Let the big picture of samsara dissolve the paper cuts of life.
steps: Frame the entire month of June as a purification retreat — even while going to work, being with friends, and living normally. Hold the container of purification intention throughout everything.

Read the Shantideva confession verses (Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life, chapter 2) once daily if possible — printed out or on your phone. Each recitation melts the veneer blocking us from admitting our negativities.

Chisel the core insight into our mental DNA: negative karma that is not purified will definitely lead to unavoidable suffering. Come back to this one point whenever we get distracted or overwhelmed by the details.
When suffering arises, notice whether it can be transformed through lojong. Reserve the strongest wisdom fear for what cannot easily be transformed: delusions hijacking the mind and lower rebirth.
practice.quote: Negative karma that’s not purified equals unavoidable suffering. It’s guaranteed.

commentary.title: Confession as the Main Practice
content: The three limbs of offering, prostration, and refuge are preliminary practices leading up to the main practice: the confession of non-virtue. Even refuge is still a preliminary — showing that confession is the main course, a complete and total practice. All Dharma is within confession.

The full and proper completion of purification depends on four opponent powers: regret, reliance, the opponent force, and the power of promise. These are not isolated practices — they’re one practice with four facets, like a concerto with four movements. Without the opponent force, regret becomes despair. Without reliance, regret becomes terror. Without the promise to change, the first three don’t land at all — because if we have no decision to change, we don’t actually regret. KK encouraged treating June as a purification retreat, holding that container throughout everything we do.

commentary.title: The Power of Regret: Admitting the Negativity
content: The first step in purifying is to admit to ourselves that our actions were negative and harmful. This sincere admission — both of harm to others and to ourselves — allows the process of uprooting negativities to begin. But something in us resists admitting. What are we protecting? Who are we hiding it from? It’s just ourselves.

Geshe-la taught that the Tibetan word for confession means to crack open a rotten log and expose it to the sun. When we hide our negativity, we’re protecting the self we normally see — protecting our samsara. When we open it up to Buddha’s love, like warm healing rays, the rot starts to dry up swiftly. But if we close it and hide it, it festers.

Part of our resistance is psychological defense. Part is not knowing how to purify. Part is blaming ourselves instead of the delusions. And part is simply not remembering — we have negativities from past lives that we can’t recall. The Shantideva confession verses serve as a practice to melt the veneer blocking those memories. Recited daily, they help bring buried negativities to the surface.

commentary.title: Four Characteristics of Karma Applied to Purification
content: We can deepen our regret by applying the four general characteristics of karma to our negative actions. The results of actions are definite: negative karma will 100% lead to suffering if not purified. The results of actions increase: unpurified negative karma is growing and spreading into other crevices of our mind every day. Actions are never wasted: negative karma doesn’t expire on its own — time doesn’t remove it, death doesn’t remove it, being a nice person doesn’t remove it. There are only two ways it goes away: purification or experiencing the suffering.

KK illustrated this with the story of Queen Noh Sangma, who gained the realization of a never-returner along with 500 disciples who all developed miracle powers. When their building caught fire, they flew into the sky — but the queen understood they had all created the collective karma to die in that fire. Since the karma was already ripening, it was unavoidable. They flew back into the flames, while a poor maidservant named Gertchog, who had no miracle powers, escaped through the sewers — because she alone had not created the karma to die that day.

commentary.title: No One Gets Lucky in Samsara
content: Ben raised the question: what if we just happen to get lucky and avoid our negative karma ripening? KK acknowledged this is a real bias — living in our comfortable bubble, we feel like we might get away with it. But this feeling comes from a limited data set. We’re around people in the top 0.0001% of samsaric comfort. Even the 99th percentile — the top 1% of samsara — involves abject agony and profound mental torment.

To counterbalance this insulation, we need to expose our mind to more suffering more often. KK mentioned a dear friend who is a sincere Dharma practitioner and constantly tells him about ongoing atrocities around the world — not out of anger or worldly obsession, but to develop compassion and break through the bubble. No one gets lucky in samsara in the long run.

commentary.title: Death Is Completely Impersonal
content: Death is a completely impersonal force — the effect of karma ripening, with no person controlling it, no mercy, no volition. There is no arc or story to our life that we’re marching along. We’re simply alive because our karma right now is not ripening in the form of death. When it changes, we just die.

This is important because we unconsciously believe there’s some fairness in the universe about our journey — that we’re on this special path and death won’t interrupt it. KK suggested the meditation: ‘This dream may end today.’ When a dream ends, there’s no warning, no closure, no goodbyes. It just ceases, and we shift to another realm. Our death is like that.

Nagarjuna said: we maintain our life in the midst of thousands of conditions that threaten death. Our life force abides like a candle flame in the breeze. We can even die an untimely death before completing our lifespan if we exhaust our merit sooner than our lifespan karma.

commentary.title: Wisdom Fear and Emptiness
content: The vivid Shantideva verses about dying without purification — being seized by the messengers of the Lord of Death, looking in all directions for refuge, finding none — are designed to stoke wisdom fear. Wisdom fear is a peaceful, virtuous mind — essentially non-attachment. The key is holding the solution in mind while reflecting on the problem: this terrifying experience would come entirely from within, from karmically created mental projections.

When we think suffering comes from outside, we try to build outer security. But once we realize everything is coming from within, outer security is meaningless — the mind can create that experience regardless. This both ratchets up the fear and ratchets up the answer: all we have to do is purify the mind. Whenever we meditate on karma, we want to bring in this emptiness understanding.

commentary.title: Purification, Merit, and Blessings
content: Anne K asked why purification isn’t everyone’s main practice all the time. KK explained that we need three things: purification (removing obstacles), accumulating merit (creating the causes of enlightenment), and receiving blessings (transforming the mind through Buddha’s influence). Purification alone gives a clear slate but doesn’t create Buddhahood. Merit without purification means obstacles remain. Blessings are the ‘magic’ that stimulates realizations — because our realizations have to come from somewhere.

Lamrim specifically gives rise to the mindset that prevents us from creating new negative karma. Without Lamrim, someone doing only Vajrasattva would keep purifying but never address the root causes. So purification and Lamrim are not two things — they’re one practice. The Lamrim is already a purification practice: compassion is the most powerful purifying force in the universe. Refuge meditation deepens reliance. Death meditation fuels regret.

commentary.title: Purifying Delusions vs. Manifest Suffering
content: Sumit asked whether suffering we experience is necessarily negative karma ripening, since we can transform it through lojong. KK explained that manifest suffering isn’t the most motivating thing to purify, precisely because we can transform it. A sincere lojong practitioner can welcome suffering as fuel for compassion and renunciation.

What’s far more motivating is purifying the causes of delusions and lower rebirth — these are not easily transformed. If delusions hijack us for the rest of this life, it’s too late. Lower rebirth generally has to be waited out. David followed up asking whether it’s more important to purify delusions than actual negative actions. KK clarified that the real point is about motivation: what stokes the strongest wisdom fear? Delusions and lower rebirth, because there’s less opportunity to transform those.

commentary.title: Harm We’ve Done to Ourselves
content: Fran was moved by the MTB phrase about admitting ‘the wrongs we have done, both to ourself and others.’ She realized that when she feels negative, it’s because she created the karma to feel that way — not just because she made someone else feel like that. By buying into negative states, she’s recreating the negative karma and tendency over and over. She had always thought of her patterns as resulting from harm done to others, not from harm done to herself as well.

Kristin and Ben discussed how all the suffering we see in the world is showing us what’s in our own karma. If our mind can appear those atrocities throughout this world, then those potentials are inside us. We can’t ignore suffering and run from it — it’s showing us our own mind.

dataShares.speaker: Fran
dataShares.summary: Continuing focus on receiving blessings — asking for blessings to concentrate before meditation, during distraction, and in hard moments. The immediate effect has strengthened her faith. Also working on the difference between wanting all beings to be happy versus truly caring whether they are.

dataShares.speaker: Anne K
dataShares.summary: Mind has gotten noisier since starting a new job. Rediscovered the practice of giving problems to her spiritual guide rather than trying to solve them herself. This has made her mind much more spacious again.

dataShares.speaker: Mary Ann
dataShares.summary: Was trying to make a decision from a place of anxiety and fear. Led to practicing affectionate love on the subway — mentally introducing herself to strangers, imagining their inner goodness. One day realized: ‘I have so many friends.’ The fear of others dissolved.

dataShares.speaker: Mimi
dataShares.summary: Chose ‘samsara is suffering’ as her conception to work on, but didn’t practice it for two weeks because things were going great (Juliana’s prom, awards, graduation). Recognized a pattern of fair-weather Dharma — going for refuge deeply when suffering, forgetting when comfortable. Pivoted to taking on future suffering practice.

dataShares.speaker: Anne P
dataShares.summary: Working on non-virtuous states of mind. Identified blaming her sister for letting her dementia get worse. Through ‘roll all blame into one’ meditation, realized that negative thoughts about loved ones are like boulders on the path toward loving all living beings.

dataShares.speaker: Jose
dataShares.summary: Three points: (1) Using the mind of respect as a doorway into cherishing strangers — easier to respect than to feel cherishing. (2) Started daily water bowl offerings since the festival — a floor practice that leads naturally into seven limb prayers. (3) Pondering that going for refuge ultimately means going for refuge to emptiness — emptiness is in every practice.

dataShares.speaker: Ryan
dataShares.summary: Had beautiful water bowls on his shrine for months but kept ignoring them. Used KK’s teaching as motivation to overcome miserliness through giving practice. Started doing offerings four to five times a week. One day noticed he was smiling while pouring the water and thought: ‘This is not Ryan.’
